newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia economy to have banner year in '98-Samper.
newsitem.headline: Colombia economy to have banner year in '98-Samper.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper forecast Monday that Colombia's economy growth would accelerate in the second half of this year and said 1998 would be a "banner year".

In his weekly televised speech, Samper reiterated pledges to cut the country's soaring urban unemployment rate -- which hit 12.7 percent by the end of the first quarter of this year -- by creating 120,000 new jobs before his term ends in August 1998.

He also said rising commodities ane energy revenues, coupled with broadened government infrastructure and housing projects, would boost gross domestic product (GDP) growth. GDP growth was two percent last year, one of the lowest figures in a decade.
"With the help of sectors like the coffee industry...and the energy industry...the government is sure that the economy will recover in the second half of this year," Samper said.
"And next year, as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) chief said on his (recent) visit to Colombia, will be a banner year," he added.
Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo has forecast a 4 percent growth in Colombia's GDP this year.

Last week, IMF director-general Michel Camdessus said there was no reason why Colombia should not attain GDP growth of 6 percent "in the future" if the government tightened up its monetary and fiscal policies.
He did not, however, say when the country could expect to see such growth levels.

In his speech, Samper referred to the so-called "Jobs Summit" held last Friday. At the meeting, government ministers outlined plans to create 120,000 new jobs by dedicating more resources to infrastructure and potable water programs.

When Samper took over the presidency in August 1994, he pledged to create 1.5 million new jobs. With just 15 months to go before he steps down, Samper seems bound to fall far short of the target,independent economists say.
The analysts predict unemployment will rise to 14 percent by mid-year before dropping back to about 13.5 percent by the end of 1997.

Samper said further jobs would be created in the construction sector, saying that he would promote a house building program for working class and lower middle class families. He did not say how many homes he hoped would be built.
